items.title: Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel
items.standfirst: Hailed as ‘a rare moment of justice’, judges’ decision sets out a roadmap for assessing the question of intentThe international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states.In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent. Continue reading...

items.title: ‘Everyone struggled for this justice’: tears in court as Rohingya vindicated in Myanmar genocide ruling
items.standfirst: Relief in the immediate aftermath of a landmark ruling, but what happens next is in the hands of governments around the worldThere were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them.For almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape. More than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh. Continue reading...

items.title: Was the historic Shenzhen summit a political win or humiliation for Putin?
items.standfirst: The world watched with bated breath Thursday as the presidents of China, Russia and the United States met for 90 minutes for an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen. Each leader came to the negotiating table with their own motivations. But Russia's Vladimir Putin was seen as walking away worse off than his counterparts, with some media outlets reporting the Kremlin leader was "humiliated" during the talks.

items.title: 'Coalition of the Willing': Ukraine's allies meet in Berlin after Trump-Putin-Xi talks
items.standfirst: Ukraine's allies met Thursday for a "Coalition of the Willing" summit in Berlin with President Volodymyr Zelensky to stress solid wartime support for Kyiv and to push for a European role in any future peace talks. The meeting – co-hosted by the leaders of Germany, France and Britain – was being held shortly after unprecedented three-way talks in China between US President Donald Trump, Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping.
